subject: Communication
title: The DMIS: Stages of Cultural Sensitivity
description: A fast breakdown of The DMIS: Stages of Cultural Sensitivity for builders.

hook.text: Some people deny cultural differences exist. Others integrate them into their identity.

buildup.text: Bennett's DMIS has six stages: Denial, Defense, Minimization, Acceptance, Adaptation, and Integration.

discovery.text: Most people are stuck at Minimization — 'We're all basically the same.' It feels inclusive but erases real differences.

twist.text: True cultural competence requires moving to Adaptation — adjusting your behavior and thinking based on cultural context.

climax.text: Integration means holding multiple cultural frames at once — thinking and feeling in more than one worldview.

punchline.text: Cultural sensitivity isn't a belief. It's a skill you develop in stages.

quiz.question: What stage do most people get stuck at in the DMIS?

details.summary: Milton Bennett's Development Model of Intercultural Sensitivity describes six stages from denial through integration. People progress from ignoring cultural differences to eventually integrating multiple cultural frameworks into their identity. Growth requires experience and reflection.
details.whyItMatters: The DMIS gives you a roadmap for growth. Knowing where you are helps you identify what you need to develop next.
takeaways: Six stages from denial to integration of cultural awareness
Most people start in the ethnocentric stages
Growth requires deliberate experience and reflection

faq.question: What are the six stages of the Bennett model?
faq.answer: Denial, defense, and minimization are ethnocentric stages. Acceptance, adaptation, and integration are ethnorelative stages. Most people begin between denial and minimization. Progression requires challenging experiences, guided reflection, and sustained cross-cultural interaction.

faq.question: Can you skip stages or regress in the model?
faq.answer: Regression is possible, especially under stress or when experiencing culture shock. Skipping stages is rare because each builds on the previous. A traumatic cross-cultural experience can temporarily push someone back to defensive or minimization stages.
